title: Gluten in unexpected places
subtitle: A shared-kitchen check, from sponges to spreads.
intro: Gluten-free ingredients are only part of the picture. Cross-contact happens when gluten transfers from another food or object.

cards.title: A sponge can carry crumbs
cards.body: A sponge or dishcloth used on gluten-containing food can transfer residue to dishes. Use a separate clean sponge or cloth for gluten-free cookware. Wash dishes thoroughly with warm, soapy water and rinse; a quick rinse alone is not enough.

cards.title: Check the shared spreads
cards.body: A knife used on regular bread can leave crumbs in butter or jam. Use a separate gluten-free spread and clean utensils.

cards.title: Look beyond the ingredients
cards.body: Shared bread toasters, pasta water, and oil used for breaded food can transfer gluten. Use separate equipment where needed, fresh pasta water, and a fryer that is not shared with gluten-containing food. Heat does not remove gluten.

kitchen_check.question: You’re making a gluten-free snack. Someone offers to wash your plate with the sponge just used to wipe up bread crumbs. What could you do?

options.text: Use the same sponge after a quick rinse
options.feedback: A quick rinse may leave gluten-containing residue. Choose a separate clean sponge or cloth and wash the plate thoroughly.

options.text: Ask for a separate clean sponge or cloth
options.feedback: Yes—then wash the plate with warm, soapy water and rinse. Check your utensils and preparation area too.

options.text: Skip washing because the plate looks clean
options.feedback: Appearance alone doesn’t tell you whether gluten has transferred. Use properly cleaned dishes and utensils.

teaching_point: Check what touches your food—not just what goes into it.
next_step: Pick one shared item in your kitchen and talk through how to prevent gluten transfer with someone at home.

title: A knife in the shared spread
intro: A knife has been used on wheat bread and then dipped into a shared spread.

content_body.prompt: Which response best addresses the cross-contact risk?

choices.label: Use a separate spread that has not had contact with gluten, with a clean utensil.
Remove the visible crumbs and use the shared spread.
Heat the shared spread to remove the gluten.

by_choice_id.heat: Heat does not eliminate gluten. Use a spread that has not had contact with gluten.
by_choice_id.crumbs: Removing visible crumbs does not establish that the spread is gluten-free. Choose a separate spread instead.
by_choice_id.separate: A separate spread and clean utensil help prevent gluten from transferring to your food.

safety_issues.heat: Heating does not make gluten-contaminated food safe.
safety_issues.crumbs: Gluten may remain in the shared spread.

teaching_point: Prevent transfer by checking both the food and the utensils used with it.

title: Choose your way to ask
intro: You want to ask the host about the food plan. You can choose how to start the conversation.

content_body.prompt: Which approach would fit you today?

choices.label: Send a message ahead of time.
Have a quiet conversation with the host.
Ask a trusted person to help start the conversation.

by_choice_id.talk: A quiet conversation may suit you. You can choose a moment when the host has time to listen.
by_choice_id.message: A message gives you time to choose your words. You could start by asking when the host has time to talk about the food plan.
by_choice_id.support: Asking someone to help is a reasonable option. You can decide together what you want to ask and how much you want to say.

teaching_point: You can choose a communication approach that fits your needs.
source_organization: Plan My C-Day — editorial test scenario

title: What would help today?
intro: Pause and notice what kind of support you would welcome today. There is no right answer.

content_body.prompt: Which feels closest to what you need?

choices.label: A little space before I make a plan.
Someone who will listen.
One small next step.
I am not sure yet.

by_choice_id.step: You chose one small step. Consider picking a single thing you would like support with, rather than working out the whole day.
by_choice_id.space: You chose a little space. You can pause and return to planning when you feel ready; you do not have to solve everything in this moment.
by_choice_id.listen: You chose someone who will listen. You might tell a trusted person, “Could you listen for a minute before we think about solutions?”
by_choice_id.unsure: Not knowing yet is a valid response. You can notice how you feel now and check in again later.

teaching_point: Your support needs can change from day to day.
source_organization: Plan My C-Day — editorial test scenario

title: Are the Fries Really Gluten-Free?
intro: You're getting burgers with friends. The menu marks the fries GF. The server says, “They're gluten-free. They're just potatoes.”

choices.label: Order them. Potatoes are naturally gluten-free.
Ask whether they're cooked in a dedicated gluten-free fryer.
Decide you can never eat restaurant fries.

by_choice_id.A: Potatoes are naturally gluten-free, but preparation matters too. Fries may share cooking oil with foods containing gluten.
by_choice_id.B: Good information-gathering. You're checking both the food itself and how it is prepared.
by_choice_id.C: You don't necessarily have to rule out all restaurant fries. Asking how they're prepared can give you more information.

teaching_point: Ingredients are only part of the question. Preparation matters too.

title: The Gluten-Free Pizza
intro: A pizza restaurant offers a gluten-free crust. Your friends are ready to order.

content_body.prompt: Which question gives you the most useful additional information?

choices.label: Does the crust contain gluten?
How is the gluten-free pizza prepared and cooked compared with your regular pizzas?
Does the pizza taste good?

by_choice_id.A: Useful, but the restaurant has already identified the crust as GF. You still don't know how the pizza is prepared.
by_choice_id.B: This gives you information about preparation—not just the crust itself.
by_choice_id.C: Important for dinner, maybe—but not for understanding cross-contact.

teaching_point: “Gluten-free ingredient” and “how was it prepared?” are two different questions.

title: Label Detective
intro: You're holding an unfamiliar packaged snack.

choices.label: Look only at the front of the package.
Use a consistent label-checking process and look at the relevant labeling and ingredient information.
Assume an unfamiliar ingredient contains gluten.

by_choice_id.A: Front-of-package claims can be useful, but don't make them your only source of information.
by_choice_id.B: Exactly. A repeatable process makes label checking easier and more reliable.
by_choice_id.C: An unfamiliar name doesn't automatically mean gluten. When information is insufficient, the answer can be Needs More Information.

teaching_point: Don't guess from how an ingredient sounds. Check reliable information.

title: Hotel Breakfast Buffet
intro: There are eggs, fruit, yogurt, toast, cereal and waffles. Some foods may naturally be gluten-free, but everything is served in the same breakfast area.

choices.label: Look at the setup and ask staff about ingredients and preparation.
Choose packaged or otherwise identifiable options you feel comfortable with.
Use food you brought if you don't get enough information to feel comfortable.
Combine any of these depending on the situation.

by_choice_id.A: That can give you information about both the foods and how they're handled.
by_choice_id.B: That can be a reasonable strategy too.
by_choice_id.C: A backup is another valid option. It doesn't mean you failed.
by_choice_id.D: Exactly. Real-life celiac management often involves combining strategies.

teaching_point: Assess the food, preparation environment and information available—then decide what works for you.

title: The Shared Snack Bowl
intro: Someone pours gluten-free chips into a communal bowl. People are also eating pizza and other snacks and reaching into different foods.

choices.label: They're GF chips, so nothing else matters.
If available, get some directly from the package or a separate serving.
Never eat chips at parties.

by_choice_id.A: The original food matters, but what happens after it's opened and served can matter too.
by_choice_id.B: That can reduce uncertainty about shared handling.
by_choice_id.C: You don't need a universal rule. Think about the particular setup.

teaching_point: Cross-contact can happen during serving—not only cooking.

title: Your Friend's Mom Cooked for You
intro: Your friend's mom says, “I made this gluten-free especially for you!” You appreciate that she tried, but you don't know how it was prepared.

choices.label: Thank you so much. Could I ask you a couple questions about how you made it?
Thank you! Would you mind showing me the ingredients you used?
I'm okay for now, but thank you so much for thinking of me.

by_choice_id.A: Appreciation and asking questions can happen at the same time.
by_choice_id.B: That's another respectful way to gather information.
by_choice_id.C: You are also allowed to decline food graciously.

teaching_point: Someone's kindness doesn't obligate you to eat. You can be appreciative and still ask questions or say no.

title: Just One Bite
intro: A friend offers you something and says, “Come on. It's literally one bite.”

content_body.prompt: Pick a response that sounds most like you.

choices.label: I have celiac, so I actually can't cheat with gluten—but I'm good.
No thanks. I need to stay gluten-free.
I'll pass. You eat it!

by_choice_id.A: That works. It's clear and gives a brief explanation.
by_choice_id.B: That works too. A short boundary is enough.
by_choice_id.C: Also reasonable. You don't owe everyone a long explanation.

teaching_point: The best script is one you can actually imagine yourself using.

title: They Got Your Order Wrong
intro: Your meal arrives and something about it looks different from what you discussed with the server. Everyone else has started eating.

choices.label: Eat it because sending it back would be embarrassing.
Ask the server to double-check the order and explain that you have celiac disease and need it gluten-free.
Say nothing and don't eat.

by_choice_id.A: Other people's meals starting doesn't change the information you need about yours.
by_choice_id.B: Speaking up here is appropriate. You can be polite and still be clear.
by_choice_id.C: You can choose not to eat, but asking may give you information or allow the restaurant to correct the problem.

teaching_point: It's okay to pause the situation when you need information.

title: Surprise Food at School
intro: Someone brings homemade cookies to class and tells you, “They're gluten-free—I think.” There is no package or label.

choices.label: Eat one because they probably checked.
Ask about ingredients and preparation. If you still don't have enough information, choose another option.
Tell everyone homemade food is unsafe for people with celiac.

by_choice_id.B: This lets you gather information without assuming either that it's safe or unsafe.
by_choice_id.C: Homemade doesn't automatically mean unsafe. The issue is whether you have enough reliable information.

teaching_point: Uncertainty is a cue to gather information—not to guess.

title: How Much Do I Have to Explain?
intro: Someone asks, “Why can't you just have a little gluten?”

content_body.prompt: What sounds most like you today?

choices.label: I have celiac disease. Gluten triggers an immune reaction, so I need to avoid it.
It's a medical diet. I have to stay gluten-free.
I'd rather not get into it right now.
Want the long version or the 10-second version?

by_choice_id.A: A clear explanation is one option.
by_choice_id.B: A short explanation can be enough.
by_choice_id.C: You are allowed to set a boundary.
by_choice_id.D: Humor can work too if it feels natural to you.

teaching_point: You decide how much of your health story you want to explain. Self-advocacy includes boundaries.

title: Tomorrow's Pizza Party
intro: Your teacher announces a pizza party for tomorrow.

content_body.prompt: What could help you feel prepared?

choices.label: Find out what's being ordered and ask about options.
Arrange a food or snack backup you know works for you.
Talk with the teacher ahead of time about what you need.
Combine these strategies.

by_choice_id.A: Knowing the plan can help you decide what you need.
by_choice_id.B: A backup can reduce pressure in the moment.
by_choice_id.C: Planning with an adult can be useful.
by_choice_id.D: Often the best plan uses more than one tool.

teaching_point: A small amount of planning beforehand can prevent a much harder decision in the moment.

title: Road Trip, Nothing Nearby
intro: Your group stops somewhere you haven't researched.

choices.label: Check the available options and ask focused questions.
Use your backup snack or food.
See whether there's another practical option nearby.
Combine these strategies.

by_choice_id.A: That may give you enough information to decide.
by_choice_id.C: That can be reasonable if time and the group allow.

teaching_point: A backup plan creates flexibility; it isn't a failure to find food.

title: Team Dinner After the Game
intro: Your teammates spontaneously decide to go out after a game.

choices.label: Go and investigate what might work.
Suggest a place you already know.
Use a backup or eat separately and still join everyone.

by_choice_id.A: You can gather information once you arrive or before ordering.
by_choice_id.B: A familiar option may lower the planning load.
by_choice_id.C: Social participation can still be the goal.

teaching_point: Food is one part of the event. Staying socially included can still be a goal even when eating isn't.

title: Everyone Changed Restaurants
intro: Your friends suddenly change the restaurant.

choices.label: Do a quick focused check of the new restaurant.
Suggest one of your known options.
Eat separately or use a backup but still join them.
Ask your friends to help find somewhere everyone can use.

by_choice_id.A: A focused check may be enough to decide your next step.
by_choice_id.B: It's okay to offer an alternative.
by_choice_id.C: That can preserve the social plan.
by_choice_id.D: Planning doesn't have to fall entirely on you.

teaching_point: Adapt based on safety, energy, time and what matters to you that day.
source_organization: Meyer & Naveh self-management framework; teen lived-experience extension

title: Birthday Cake Moment
intro: You're going to a birthday party tomorrow and don't know whether there will be a gluten-free dessert.

choices.label: Ask ahead.
Bring something you enjoy.
Go without worrying about dessert.
Make another plan that works for you.

by_choice_id.A: Knowing what to expect may make the event easier.
by_choice_id.B: A backup can help you participate without uncertainty.
by_choice_id.C: Dessert doesn't have to determine whether you enjoy the party.
by_choice_id.D: Your plan can fit your priorities.

teaching_point: Planning is about giving yourself options—not making every event revolve around food.
source_organization: Meyer & Naveh self-management framework; Celiac Disease Foundation

title: Cross-Contact: What Actually Happens?
subtitle: Gluten-free food can pick up gluten along the way.

cards.body: Cross-contact happens when a food that is gluten-free comes into contact with gluten. It can happen during growing, processing, storage, preparation, or serving.
cards.title: 1 | The basic idea

cards.body: A food can start with gluten-free ingredients and still be affected by how it is handled. Shared utensils, preparation surfaces, serving areas, or other food-contact situations can matter.
cards.title: 2 | Think beyond ingredients

cards.body: Your job is to gather the information that matters for the situation. Ask what the food contains and how it was prepared or served. If you still don't have enough information, you can choose another option.
cards.title: 3 | Your job isn't to panic

content_body.source_evidence: NIDDK — Eating, Diet, & Nutrition for Celiac Disease

title: Shared Fryers
subtitle: The potato isn't the only thing to check.

cards.body: Plain potatoes are naturally gluten-free. But restaurant fries may be cooked in the same oil as breaded foods or other foods containing gluten.
cards.title: 1 | Fries can be tricky

cards.body: Try: “Are the fries cooked in a dedicated gluten-free fryer?” You can also ask whether the fries themselves have any coating or seasoning that needs checking.
cards.title: 2 | Ask one high-value question

cards.body: Not every restaurant fryer setup is the same. Get the information for the place you're actually at.
cards.title: 3 | Don't make a universal rule

title: Reading a Food Label
subtitle: Use a process instead of guessing.

cards.body: Check the package for a gluten-free claim and read the ingredient information. In the U.S., “gluten-free” is a voluntary claim, but foods using it under FDA rules must meet the federal definition.
cards.title: 1 | Start with the label

cards.body: Gluten occurs naturally in wheat, barley, rye, and their crossbred hybrids such as triticale. Ingredients derived from gluten-containing grains can also require attention.
cards.title: 2 | Know the major grains

cards.body: If you cannot tell whether an ingredient or product works for your gluten-free diet, don't guess from the name. Look for reliable information, such as the manufacturer or another trusted source.
cards.title: 3 | Unknown doesn't mean unsafe—or safe

content_body.source_evidence: FDA — Gluten and Food Labeling; NIDDK

title: Naturally GF vs. Prepared GF
subtitle: A naturally gluten-free food can change once preparation starts.

cards.body: Many foods are naturally gluten-free, including plain fruits, vegetables, rice, potatoes, meat, and fish.
cards.title: 1 | Naturally gluten-free

cards.body: Once a food is seasoned, coated, mixed, cooked, or served with other foods, ingredients and cross-contact may need to be checked.
cards.title: 2 | Prepared food adds questions

cards.body: Ask: “What is in it?” and “How was it prepared?” Those two questions solve different parts of the puzzle.
cards.title: 3 | Use two questions

title: Eating Out: The Questions That Matter
subtitle: You don't need 20 questions. Start with the ones that change your decision.

cards.body: Let the server know you have celiac disease and need a gluten-free meal. A clear medical explanation can help staff understand that this is not simply a preference.
cards.title: 1 | Tell them what you need

cards.body: Useful questions include: What is in the dish? How is it prepared? Is shared oil or equipment used? Is there a separate or cleaned preparation process for gluten-free food?
cards.title: 2 | Ask about ingredients + preparation

cards.body: A restaurant conversation cannot guarantee a meal. It can give you information to make your own decision. A backup remains an option.
cards.title: 3 | Decide from the information you get

content_body.source_evidence: NIDDK; Beyond Celiac; Celiac Disease Foundation
